25: After 1857 and the Crown takeover of 1858, the Secretary of State in London is the Top Boss. Charles Wood: 'despotism controlled from home', until 1947. Not a democracy.

In 1861 the State is rebuilt: ICA 1861 restructures Legislature and Executive, the Indian High Courts Act 1861 the Judiciary. The Governor-General's Council splits into VEC (executive) and ILC (law-making).
The VEC adds 6 to 12 additional members for law-making and the room becomes the ILC. Every VEC member sits in the ILC, so officials stay in majority. Provinces copy this.
Canning56-62 starts the Portfolio System in 1859; ICA 1861 makes it law. Finance member James Wilson after the 1857 debt, so VEC = GG + 5 + C-I-C. Public Works 1874.
The Viceroy nominates 6 to 12 additional members, half non-officials. For the first time non-officers make law: three Indians in 1862, rewarding 1857 loyalists. Only 45 Indians until 1892.
The VEC alone is 7 (GG + 5 + C-I-C), more than the most non-officials possible (6). With 6 additional members: 10 officials against 3 non-officials. 'Official' means pro-British bureaucrat.
The ILC has almost no powers: no questions, no resolutions, no budget vote, bills only with the Viceroy's approval. He holds an absolute veto and a 6-month ordinance.
The Charter Act 1833 took Bombay and Madras law-making to the Centre. ICA 1861 gives it back and plans PLCs (Bengal 1862, NWP 1886, Punjab 1897). Centre's share: 100% to 90%.
BRASS: the Viceroy keeps five keys: sanctioning nominations, framing rules, approving bills, one budget, creating provinces. They end only in 1892, 1919, 1935. One hand gives, the other takes.

Centralisation began 1773, peaked 1833; decentralisation began 1861; Provincial Autonomy 1935. Elections come step by step: 1909, then 1919. ICA 1861 fails the teacher's test of responsible government.
26: The opponent was a foreign State, so the Moderates' Step 1 was to limit it with a good Constitution, drawing on Utilitarianism (laws) and Liberalism (rights, rule of law).

Constitutional methods mean only the State's own channels: elections, Legislature, Judiciary, RTI, petitions. Gandhi's Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience are outside, extra-constitutional mass struggle.

They called British rule exploitative but trusted British Providence. Goal: Limited Self-Government within British rule, as masses were not ready. Banerjea: end 'Un-British Rule'; Bonnerjee: INC loyal to the British.

Four political asks (abolish India Council, 50% indirect election in councils, real powers, Indianise services) and seven economic (cut military spending, lower land revenue, no Salt Tax...). None met.
First session 1885: 72 delegates, mostly Bombay and Madras, all upper-caste Western-educated professionals. Hindus 90%, Muslims about 6.5% against 20% in the census. Tyabji was the exception.
Calcutta 1886, under Dadabhai Naoroji: the INC avoids social questions until 1907 to keep unity. In 1893 it stayed silent on cow-killing riots and Muslim participation fell.
In 1892-1905 about 20% were landlords, 40% lawyers, 15% traders, all part-time. So no anti-Zamindar stand, they opposed the Punjab Land Alienation Bill 1900, and backed Indian capital over labour.

Lancashire makers lobbied for factory rules to raise Indian costs; Moderates said infant industries needed room. Factories Act 1881 (Ripon 80-84), 1891 (Lansdowne 88-94), Mines Act 1901 (Curzon 99-05). Verdict: complex.
They sent prayers and petitions, passed resolutions, used the press, and avoided mass action. The teacher's 3P: Prayer, Petitions, Protests in the press. Critics called it the Strategy of Mendicancy.

They did not represent the masses and distrusted them, so would not mobilise them. A movement neither representing nor threatening could be ignored. Four power factors: claim, masses, demands, methods.

Gokhale (1913): without these methods the British would not have let the INC function. Goal moved: Limited Self-Government 1885-1906, Self-Government 1906, Dominion Status 1916, 1928, Purna Swaraj 1929.
27: At the first INC session, Bombay 1885, the goal was national unity. India had regions, languages, castes and religions but no single political community, so building one came before demanding rights.
1886: Naoroji's rule, only political questions, so the fight is Indians against British. 1888: a veto if the Hindu or Muslim majority disagrees. 1889: the Minority Clause for reserved seats.
Each session was in a different region and the President never came from the host region. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta builds all-India leadership and inter-regional bonds.
The President acted like a Speaker; members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions, new for India. Lok Sabha procedures have roots in INC sessions: the modern political era began with the INC.

The Moderates were pro-industrialisation, not anti-poor. Every industrial country rose on its capitalists; communist industrialisation came only in 1917. Indian capitalists struggled against British imports.

After ICA 1892 disappointed them, the Moderates built the Drain Theory: Britain used political control for its own gain, so the White Man's Burden was false. Naoroji 1901, R.C. Dutt 1902, 1904, Ranade.

Before British industrialisation India exported finished goods. Afterwards it supplied raw materials (cotton, indigo, jute, opium) and bought British goods. Handicrafts died and artisans crowded into agriculture.
Steam engine (1769) brought machines, ships, railways; Suez Canal (1859-69) cut 4,500 miles. Railways built under Dalhousie 48-56 for the army carried raw materials out and finished goods in.
Before 1813 the drain was Dastak misuse, Plassey plunder 1757-65, land revenue from 1765. After 1813 it was policy: no protective tariff till World War I, managed exchange rate, Council Bills.

Home Charges: the bill India paid Britain for services it claimed to give (eight heads, pensions, EIC dividends, debt interest, stores...). India sold more than it bought yet lost the forex: double drain.
The teacher marks this debate 'mmp'. Britain cited railways (5% guaranteed), canals (25% irrigated) and a drain of only 2%. Naoroji: 2% was surplus capital that would compound. So: demand for Swaraj.
28: From 1885 to 1892 the Moderates used 3P (Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions). The reply was ICA 1892, the Lord Cross Act, with Lansdowne 88-94 as Viceroy: a result and proof of failure.
Indirectly nominated members in the ILC and PLCs were a first. But 'election' was left out: for 10 seats, 50 names were asked and the Viceroy or Governor chose 10.
Tier 1: District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations, Zamindars sent names to the Governor for PLCs. Tier 2: PLC members and Bengal Chamber sent names to the Viceroy for the ILC.
ILC additional members rose to 10 to 16 (6 to 12 in 1861), at least half non-officials. But VEC plus official members always outnumbered them: they may speak but cannot win.
The VEC did not change: GG + C-in-C + six Ordinary Members (Finance 1861, Public Works 1874). The ILC is the VEC plus additional members, one box inside the other.
For the first time members could ask questions (6 days' notice) and discuss the Budget (no vote, no amendment). No resolutions; the Viceroy kept the veto and the 6-month ordinance power.
The Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers to the PLC: the first relaxation since 1861. Rule-making, bill approval, single budget and creating provinces stayed.
On the Aitchison Commission (1886-88), in Lansdowne 88-94's time, CCS became ICS, UCS became PCS, Statutory Civil Services ended. Administrative orders, not ICA 1892: an exam trap.

Indianisation, non-official majority, elected majority, proper indirect election, powerful legislatures and constitutionalism were refused. Only expansion of the ILC and PLCs scored a yes, a dissatisfied one.
Disappointed, the Moderates asked for Dominion-style self-government (Australia 1901, Canada 1867). Swaraj became the INC goal at Calcutta 1906. With the Drain Theory, these were twin pillars.
If prayers and petitions gave only this hollow Act, the method was bankrupt. Belief in British benevolence cracked; street protest took root, with the Bengal Partition of 1905 as catalyst.
